questions.scenario: A mobile app's 'Send money' call to POST /api/v1/transfers times out after 30 seconds. The app's HTTP library is configured to retry idempotent requests automatically.
questions.question: Will the library retry this request, and why?
options: No: timeouts are never retried by HTTP clients
Yes: every HTTP method is retried after a timeout
Yes: POST is idempotent when the body is identical
No: POST is not idempotent, so a safe retry needs an Idempotency-Key that the server honours
questions.explanation: POST is neither safe nor idempotent, so generic clients do not retry it. Payment APIs make it retryable with an Idempotency-Key header that the server uses to return the original result instead of moving money twice.

questions.scenario: A transfer request is well-formed and passes validation, but the source account has insufficient funds.
questions.question: Which status code best describes the result?
options: 400 Bad Request
200 OK with {"success": false}
500 Internal Server Error
422 Unprocessable Content
questions.explanation: The request is syntactically valid but breaks a business rule, which is what 422 expresses. 400 is for malformed or invalid input, 500 for unexpected server failures, and a 200 with an error flag hides the failure from monitoring and clients.

questions.scenario: A customer requests GET /api/v1/accounts/0123456789, an account that exists but belongs to another customer.
questions.question: What should the API return to avoid leaking information?
options: 404 Not Found
200 OK with the balance masked
409 Conflict
403 Forbidden
questions.explanation: Returning 403 confirms the account number exists, which helps attackers enumerate accounts. Responding as if it does not exist (404) gives away nothing.

questions.scenario: Two support agents load the same customer profile. Agent A saves a new phone number; a minute later agent B saves a new address from the stale copy and A's change disappears.
questions.question: Which HTTP mechanism prevents this lost update?
options: ETag on GET, If-Match on the update, and 412 Precondition Failed when the version has changed
Cache-Control: no-store on the GET response
Returning 202 Accepted for every update
Using PUT instead of PATCH
questions.explanation: Conditional requests make the update depend on the version the client read. If someone saved in between, the precondition fails with 412 and the client must re-read and merge.

questions.scenario: An outbound NIP transfer is accepted by your service but will only be confirmed by the switch some seconds later.
questions.question: What is the best response to POST /api/v1/transfers?
options: 200 OK with an empty body
202 Accepted with a Location header pointing to the transfer, which the client can poll or receive a webhook for
504 Gateway Timeout until the switch replies
201 Created with status SUCCEEDED, then fix it later if the switch rejects it
questions.explanation: 202 tells the client the work is accepted but not finished, and Location gives it somewhere to check. Claiming success before the switch confirms is how customers see money 'sent' that never arrives.

questions.scenario: You are reviewing a junior engineer's API design for a wallet service.
questions.question: Which of these are design problems? (Choose two.)
options: Dates use ISO 8601 with a time zone offset
GET /api/v1/wallets/{id}/confirm-transfer moves money
Collections are named with plural nouns, such as /api/v1/wallets
Amounts are sent as JSON numbers such as 2500.1
questions.explanation: GET must be safe; prefetchers and retries would move money. Floating-point JSON numbers lose precision; send decimal strings with a currency. Plural collection nouns and ISO 8601 dates are good practice.

questions.scenario: A client sends PUT /api/v1/accounts/123/nickname with the body {"nickname": "Savings"} three times because of flaky connectivity.
questions.question: What is the server state afterwards?
options: Undefined: PUT is not idempotent
The nickname is 'Savings', exactly as after one request, because PUT replaces the state and is idempotent
Three nickname history entries and the nickname 'SavingsSavingsSavings'
The second and third requests fail with 409 Conflict
questions.explanation: PUT sets the resource to the given state, so repeating it changes nothing further. That is what makes it safe for clients to retry.
